extracted.intended_audience: journalists, editors, and readers interested in fact‑checking methodology (PolitiFact users and practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: PolitiFact's procedural and editorial standards for selecting, researching, rating, publishing, and correcting political fact‑checks, promise tracking, and consistency (Flip‑O‑Meter) analyses. Focused on transparency, independence, sourcing, and clear definitions for ratings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core principles
rubrics_metrics.description: PolitiFact’s core principles are independence, transparency, fairness, thorough reporting and clear writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These principles guide why PolitiFact publishes (to give citizens information needed to govern themselves) and inform all editorial decisions and daily practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ownership and organizational independence
rubrics_metrics.description: PolitiFact is owned by the nonprofit Poynter Institute and was transferred from the Tampa Bay Times to allow PolitiFact to function fully as a not‑for‑profit national news organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structural ties and governance (control by a single executive who picks a successor) are explained to show historical connections but also the institutional arrangements intended to protect editorial independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding disclosure and donor policy
rubrics_metrics.description: PolitiFact discloses any individual donation or grant in excess of $1,000 and organizations that contributed more than 5 percent of total PolitiFact revenues in the previous calendar year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PolitiFact does not accept anonymous donations, donations from political parties, elected officials or candidates seeking public office, or other sources considered conflicts of interest. Contracts and grant agreements include clauses asserting editorial independence; donors, advertisers or grantmakers receive no influence over content or ratings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalist ethics and political activity restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: PolitiFact journalists avoid the public expression of political opinion and public involvement in the political process (no political contributions, campaigning, online petitions, yard signs, political marches).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They also avoid expressing political views on social media, avoid snarky commentary, and may vote privately but keep votes to themselves. Policy applies to full‑time staff, correspondents and interns to prevent compromising independence and fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim selection criteria (how we choose claims to fact‑check)
rubrics_metrics.description: PolitiFact selects the most newsworthy and significant statements because they can't check everything. Each day journalists scan transcripts, speeches, news stories, press releases, campaign brochures, TV, social media, and reader submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In deciding which statements to check they consider: Is the statement rooted in a verifiable fact (not opinion)? Does it seem misleading or sound wrong? Is it significant (avoid minor 'gotchas')? Is it likely to be passed on and repeated? Would a typical person hear it and wonder if it's true? They aim to pick items from both Democrats and Republicans while more often checking the party in power or repeat offenders.

rubrics_metrics.name: On‑the‑record sourcing and source publication
rubrics_metrics.description: PolitiFact uses on‑the‑record interviews and publishes a list of sources with every fact‑check; when possible the list includes links to freely available sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They always contact or attempt to contact the person, website or organization that made the statement. Emphasis is on primary sources and original documentation (government reports, academic studies, data). If relying on another outlet that used unnamed sources, PolitiFact notes that it cannot independently verify that reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research and reporting process
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a general reporting process that often includes: reviewing what other fact‑checkers have found, a thorough Google search, searching online databases, consulting a variety of experts, reviewing publications, and a final overall review of available evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The goal is to verify information independently rather than rely on second‑hand claims or what a campaign or official says.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth‑O‑Meter rating scale
rubrics_metrics.description: The Truth‑O‑Meter reflects the relative accuracy of a statement with six ratings: TRUE, MOSTLY TRUE, HALF TRUE, MOSTLY FALSE, FALSE, PANTS ON FIRE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions given: TRUE = accurate and nothing significant missing; MOSTLY TRUE = accurate but needs clarification/additional info; HALF TRUE = partially accurate but leaves out important details or takes things out of context; MOSTLY FALSE = contains an element of truth but ignores critical facts that give a different impression; FALSE = not accurate; PANTS ON FIRE = not accurate and makes a ridiculous claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof and timing for Truth‑O‑Meter ratings
rubrics_metrics.description: The burden of proof is on the speaker, and PolitiFact rates statements based on the information known at the time the statement is made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This shapes how evidence is assessed and the temporal frame for judging accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth‑O‑Meter editorial decision process
rubrics_metrics.description: The reporter suggests a rating when they turn in the report to an assigning editor; the editor and reporter review together, then the assigning editor brings the rated fact‑check to two additional editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The three editors and reporter discuss questions such as: Is the statement literally true? Is there another way to read it? Did the speaker provide evidence? How have similar statements been handled previously? The three editors then vote on the rating (two votes carry the decision). Edits are made and the report is published.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flip‑O‑Meter rating scale and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The Flip‑O‑Meter rates an official's consistency on an issue and is not intended as a value judgment about changing positions. It has three ratings: NO FLIP (no significant change), HALF FLIP (partial change), FULL FLOP (complete change).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The analysis of the shift and degree of change is considered informative; the writing, editing and rating process for Flip‑O‑Meter reports is similar to Truth‑O‑Meter fact‑checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Campaign promise tracking and promise‑meter ratings
rubrics_metrics.description: PolitiFact tracks campaign promises to inform readers how well elected officials carry out their agenda; promises are rated based on verifiable outcomes, not intentions or effort. A promise is defined as a prospective statement of an action or outcome that is verifiable, and all promises list the source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promise meter ratings (six levels): NOT YET RATED (initial state until evidence of progress), IN THE WORKS (proposed/being considered), STALLED (no movement), COMPROMISE (substantially less than original but still a significant accomplishment consistent with original goal), PROMISE KEPT (original promise mostly/completely fulfilled), PROMISE BROKEN (promise not fulfilled). Ratings can change over time as circumstances evolve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrections, updates and editorial transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: PolitiFact corrects errors quickly with transparency and different treatments depending on severity: Major errors of fact receive a mark of correction at the top and an archived copy of previous fact‑check is preserved and linked; lesser errors of fact get a correction at the bottom; typos/grammar are corrected without a mark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corrected fact‑checks receive a tag of 'Corrections and updates.' Updates that add information (not corrections) receive an 'Corrections and updates' tag and may be added parenthetically or at the end with a date. Explanatory editor’s notes are used to alert readers to helpful information without changing the original report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance and newsworthiness in selection
rubrics_metrics.description: PolitiFact tries to select facts to check from both Democrats and Republicans, and focuses on statements about topics that are in the news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They explicitly avoid minor 'gotchas' and prioritize significance; nonetheless they more often check the party that holds power or people who repeatedly make attention‑getting or misleading statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partner sites and consistency of standards
rubrics_metrics.description: State and partner PolitiFact sites (e.g., PolitiFact Florida, PunditFact and other state partners) follow the same principles as the national site.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partners include newspapers and independent news organizations; the stated intent is consistent application of these editorial standards across partner sites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader engagement and avenues for support/contact
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers can suggest claims to fact‑check via email, join the Truth Squad membership, sign up for email, like/follow on social media, and share work; contact emails are provided for general questions and for Truth Squad membership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supporters receive communications and perks; reader suggestions are one of the inputs into claim selection and contact info for journalists is available on staff profiles to foster transparency and feedback.
